topic: Testing whether hysteresis in a ferromagnet (magnetic remanence) acts as a true physical memory mechanism for past magnetic fields, versus merely reflecting slow transient relaxation, in materials physics
stimulus: Iron remembers. You push a field through it, remove the field, and the lump stays magnetized, which is a kind of grudge. But is it memory or just slow forgetting? Physicists sort this out with first-order reversal curves, a lovely trick: you saturate the sample, back off to some reversal field, then sweep up again, and repeat from many starting points. The result is a map, a Preisach distribution, of tiny two-state switches called hysterons, each with its own up and down thresholds. It reminds me of a crowd of stubborn voters. Then there's return-point memory, where the material retraces a minor loop exactly and seems to remember the extremes of its history, like a stack of nested parentheses. Wiping property: smaller excursions get erased when a larger one passes. That's odd, because the memory is in the ordering of maxima, not the timing. Meanwhile, magnetic viscosity muddies things: remanence decays roughly logarithmically with time, so ask again later and the answer changes. Thermal activation over barriers, Néel relaxation, blocking temperature. Rocks do the same thing, and paleomagnetists read ancient fields from lava, sometimes warming samples stepwise to peel away later overprints. Thellier experiments! Heat, cool in a known field, compare. Coin-sorters, shape-memory alloys, crumpled Mylar sheets and sheared foams also learn amplitudes, apparently. Does a paper clip bent back and forth remember? Fatigue says yes, grimly.

topic: Whether hysteresis in a ferromagnet (or a material's magnetic domain state) acts as a physical memory mechanism: how to test that a transient field leaves a lasting, readable trace in the material, rather than just a lingering effect of the present conditions
stimulus: Magnets remember, supposedly, but the first oddity is that a piece of iron has no brain and no clock, only a history written into where its domain walls got stuck. Physicists draw the hysteresis loop, that fat lopsided oval, and read memory off the gap between going up and coming down. But a gap alone could be slow relaxation, so they wait, and wait, and watch remanence decay logarithmically, which is a clue that there are many barriers, not one. Then the wiping tricks: demagnetize with a shrinking AC field and the loop's memory spirals to nothing, like erasing a chalkboard with gentler and gentler strokes. Oddly the reverse is also true, since first-order reversal curves let you read out the whole distribution of tiny switching units, a fossil census. Paleomagnetists lean on this, reading ancient lava as a compass frozen at cooling time, though a later lightning strike can overwrite it, so they heat in steps to peel layers back like onion skin. Return-point memory sounds like a fairy tale: cycle partway, come back, and the system retraces exactly. Shape-memory alloys and crumpled paper do something similar, and Preisach models treat the whole thing as a crowd of little switches with two thresholds each. Is the memory in the switches or in their coupling? Spin glasses ask that too, with their aging and rejuvenation, temperature dips remembered like stubborn grudges.

topic: Testing whether hysteresis in a ferromagnet (or magnetic recording medium) is truly a memory mechanism: how physicists decide that a material's past field exposure is stored in its domain structure rather than just transiently lingering
stimulus: Hysteresis loops are the first thing anyone draws, and they're a little deceptive, because a loop only says the present depends on the past, not that anything is being kept. A slow-relaxing paramagnet can fake it if you sweep fast enough. So people start varying the sweep rate, and the loop's width changes, which is a clue that time matters, that "memory" is partly just sluggishness. Then there's the first-order reversal curve trick: climb partway up, come back down, map the whole family of little returns, and suddenly you see a Preisach plane, a census of tiny bistable switches, each with its own up-threshold and down-threshold. Memory as a crowd of cheap two-state units. That reminds me of return-point memory, where the material remembers the extremum of a history even after being wiggled inside it, like wiping out a cache only when you exceed the old peak. Barkhausen noise: you can hear domain walls snapping, pinned on defects, crackling like a fire. The memory is literally in the dirt, the pinning sites. Demagnetize with an AC field decaying slowly and the record vanishes, which is how you test erasure. Spin glasses do something stranger: age them, and they remember temperature pauses as dips in the curve. Old tape drifts, print-through bleeds between layers on a reel. Thermal stability of a hard drive bit gets a number, the KV over kT ratio, and everyone argues about ten years versus a century.

topic: Testing whether hysteresis in a ferromagnetic material (or a spin-glass) acts as a genuine physical memory mechanism, i.e., how physicists decide that a material's past field history is stored in its domain structure rather than just lingering transient effects
stimulus: Iron remembers. That's the odd thing about a paperclip that gets magnetized by a passing magnet: nothing in its chemistry changed, yet the past is written into it. Physicists draw the hysteresis loop, that fat lopsided curve, and the area inside it is energy lost as the domains snap around, so memory costs heat. Barkhausen noise comes to mind: put a coil around the sample and listen, and you hear crackling as domain walls jump past pinning sites, like a crowd of tiny ratchets. Each crackle is a little decision. Then there are first-order reversal curves, where you saturate, back off to some reversal field, and sweep up again, mapping which grains flipped and which stayed put. It's like interrogating the material with different histories to see which ones it distinguishes. Spin glasses are stranger: the memory-and-rejuvenation experiments where you cool, pause at a temperature, resume, and later on warming the dip in susceptibility reappears, as if the system had kept a hidden ledger of every pause. Return-point memory shows up in Preisach models, a pile of imaginary two-state switches each with its own thresholds. A suspicion lurks: is the stored thing a state, or just slow relaxation, aging that merely looks like remembering? Annealing erases it, shaking with an AC field demagnetizes, and the trouble is that crumpled paper, sheared sand, and charge-density waves all show similar tricks. Even coffee-ground jammed packings seem to remember how they were tapped.

topic: Testing whether a material (e.g., a ferromagnet or shape-memory alloy) exhibits hysteresis-based memory of past conditions, rather than just responding to present conditions: what measurements would show that the history of applied stress or field is stored in the material's state?
stimulus: Hysteresis loops are the obvious place to start, that lazy fat curve where going up and coming down don't retrace each other. But a loop alone doesn't prove memory, because friction or lag could fake it. So people sweep slower and slower, and if the loop survives in the quasi-static limit it's rate-independent, which is the real signature. Then there's the oddity of return-point memory: cycle a magnet inside a minor loop and it remembers the turning points, like a stack of nested bookmarks, and erases them when you exceed a bigger extremum. Wiping rules! Preisach models treat the material as a crowd of tiny bistable switches, each flipping at its own threshold, which makes me think of coin-sorting machines. Kids learn about this with crumpled paper, which keeps its creases. Then Keim and Nagel's work on memory in sheared or cyclically driven suspensions: you train a system at one amplitude and read the amplitude back out later, like a tape recorder made of mud. Reading out is destructive sometimes, which is irritating. Annealing erases it, so does heating past a critical temperature. Shape-memory alloys, meanwhile, remember by crystal phase, not by switches, and that's a different mechanism wearing the same costume. Aging in glasses shows memory too, via the Kovacs effect, where volume relaxes non-monotonically after a temperature jump. Why does that feel like a clue?

topic: Testing whether hysteresis in a magnetic material (e.g., a ferromagnet or rock's remanent magnetization) acts as a true physical memory of past fields, rather than just a transient response to current conditions
stimulus: Paleomagnetists treat a rock as a tape recorder, and the first oddity is that the tape is always partly erased. Magnetite grains lock in the field at cooling, but then viscous drift creeps in, lightning strikes overwrite patches, and burial heat rewrites the rest. So the question is never "is there memory?" but "which memory is this, and how old?" Stepwise thermal demagnetization peels layers like an onion: heat to 200°C, measure, heat to 300°C, measure again, and watch the vector walk toward the origin on a Zijderveld plot. A straight line heading home means a single clean imprint. A kink means two eras are stacked. I love that kink. It feels like a palimpsest. Then there's the return-point memory in hysteresis loops, where a ferromagnet seems to "remember" the extremes of its history, the way a wiped-down whiteboard keeps ghost lines. Preisach models treat it as a crowd of tiny two-state switches, each flipping at its own threshold. That sounds oddly like voting. And the FORC diagrams, those first-order reversal curves, map the crowd's distribution. Meanwhile spin glasses do aging: wait longer, and the response slows. Does the system remember how long it sat? Fold tests and conglomerate tests ask whether the signal predates the tilting of the beds. Pebbles pointing in random directions mean the magnetism came after. Memory dated by geometry, which is strange and nice.

topic: Testing whether hysteresis in a ferromagnet (magnetic memory) is a genuine memory mechanism: what measurements show that a material's past field history is stored in its domain structure, rather than just reflecting a transient lag
stimulus: Hysteresis loops are the obvious first thing, but a loop alone is oddly ambiguous: a slow relaxation would also trace one if you sweep fast enough. So people vary the sweep rate and watch whether the loop collapses to a limit, the rate-independent part being the real memory. Then there are first-order reversal curves, where you saturate, back off to some reversal field, and sweep up again, building a map of little switching units, each with its own up-threshold and down-threshold. That map is basically a census of tiny bistable things, which sounds like Preisach's picture, and the return-point memory it predicts is weirdly specific: the system remembers the nested extrema of its history and forgets the rest, like a stack. Wiping is a related trick. Demagnetize with a decaying AC field and the memory goes, though sometimes it goes only partway. Thermal tests come next: heat it past the Curie point and the record vanishes entirely, so memory is tied to order. Yet a spin glass keeps aging, and a rejuvenation-and-memory experiment pauses cooling at one temperature and finds a dip in susceptibility that returns on reheating, a ghost of the pause. Barkhausen noise crackles as domain walls snap past pinning defects, and paleomagnetists read this very property in basalt, where cooled lava preserves ancient fields. Meanwhile the defects are the memory, quietly.

topic: Testing whether hysteresis in ferromagnetic materials (e.g., a magnetic domain pattern) is a genuine memory mechanism: how physicists decide whether a material's past magnetic field history is stored in its internal state, rather than just lingering transient effects
stimulus: Iron remembers, supposedly. Push a field up, pull it back to zero, and the magnetization doesn't return; the loop stays open. But physicists get suspicious of the word memory almost immediately, because a slowly decaying transient looks the same on a short afternoon. So you wait, you watch relaxation, you find magnetic viscosity, logarithmic creep, and suddenly forgetting is itself a process with a clock. Then there's the old tape-recorder idea: first-order reversal curves, FORC diagrams, where you ride up to a reversal field and come back down, mapping a whole landscape of little switching units, each with its own coercivity and its own bias. It's like interrogating a crowd by asking different questions in different orders. Return-point memory is the odd one: cycle inside a loop and the material returns exactly to where it was at the turning point, as though it kept a ledger. Spin glasses do something stranger, remembering temperatures through aging dips, a Kaplan-style pause that leaves a notch in the curve. And crumpled paper, sheared foams, and coffee-ground suspensions are said to do the same, which makes me wonder about the word material. Demagnetizing with a decaying AC field erases the ledger, yet Barkhausen noise, crackling in a pickup coil, suggests avalanches replay the same sites. Is the memory in the domain walls, pinned on defects, or in the defects themselves? Old rocks keep paleomagnetic stripes for billions of years, which is a different kind of patience.
